prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B004 as my preferred configuration after the full exchange. The scientific core has not been challenged by anyone: the Kane-Mele Z2 classification identified a symmetry-protected phase that cannot be reached adiabatically from an ordinary insulator, and Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe wells gave a quantitative signature (conductance close to 2e^2/h from helical edge channels, with the expected dependence on width and gate) that independent groups later reproduced in other systems and extended to three-dimensional materials by ARPES. The Z2 class exists only because time-reversal symmetry and strong spin-orbit coupling are present; it has no counterpart in the magnetic-field-driven integer quantum Hall states or the Haldane chain, which is the central point of distinction from the 2016 prize. It is also a result that my own community now relies on daily, since first-principles prediction of topological band inversion is routine in materials theory. I am not blind to the fact that B006 has the strongest backing of any ballot: it is mature and cleanly credited, and I will be able to support it without reservation if the committee concludes that attribution on B004 cannot be settled. My position stays with B004 because I think the discovery of a new state of matter should weigh somewhat more than an improved measurement when both are mature, but I hold that as a judgment, not a certainty.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the real weakness and round 1 sharpened it rather than resolving it. Three colleagues (Danielsson, Kroll, Johansson) say the trio stitches Kane and Mele's theory to an experiment that was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and with Zhang's death in 2018 the committee cannot repair that by adding him. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is defensible on a rule of crediting the original idea and the first decisive experiment, but the HgTe proposal was a necessary link and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan sits partly outside the citation. I also concede that the sole supporter of a ballot that seven others list only as an alternative should be cautious: if the expert reports cannot settle the HgTe-proposal question, B006 or B009 would face fewer objections on credit.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio stitches a theory prize to an experiment proposed by other theorists, that Zhang's death leaves a sequence completed by people the committee cannot name, and that he would want an expert report before ranking B004 above B043.
responses.response: That is the strongest objection to my ballot and I do not dismiss it. My answer is that the prize has long recognised the decisive theoretical concept and the first decisive experiment when the proposal for a specific platform is a step between them, as long as the citation says what is being recognised; the citation I now propose names the Z2 class and the quantum spin Hall effect, with the HgTe observation as the experimental proof, and so does not claim the platform proposal. But I agree the point is not mine alone to settle and I support an expert report on whether Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang changed what Molenkamp measured or only told him where to look. On B043 itself, I accept your point that the diffuse flux is independently confirmed, but my doubts over source identification and the long precursor history mean I would put it behind B004 and B006 on present evidence.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B009, defends keeping Bistritzer beside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and says B004 has the harder allocation problem because Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the three-dimensional work are outside the three names.
responses.response: I agree with Mehlig on Bistritzer: the 2011 paper is a joint two-author calculation and I withdraw the suggestion in my round-1 file that the trio might be redrawn; if B009 is chosen all three names should stay. I also accept that B009 has a more compact prediction-to-experiment chain than B004. Where I differ is maturity and what is credited. The pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is unsettled and the field is eight years old, and an experimental credit that omits Yuan Cao and the Dean, Young and Yacoby groups is no tidier than my own. I would regard B009 as a prize for the next cycle or two, which is why I keep it as an alternative, but it is the one I would back if the committee wanted a condensed-matter part that rests on a clean theoretical derivation.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B009 pairs a compact original prediction with a first decisive experiment that many groups have reproduced, that the field is still opening, and that B006 would be the safer choice if the committee wants a mature, simply attributed invention.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson that the experimental reproducibility of correlated and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene is not in doubt, and that a citation should be worded around observed phenomena, not an unresolved mechanism. Where we differ is on whether to wait, and I would say what would move me: a resolution within a few years of the pairing question, or a second platform with a clean result, would turn my alternative into a preferred ballot. I also take her point that B006 is the safer choice on attribution and maturity, and I note that she and I hold the same two ballots as alternatives for the same reason. On sequence, the Z2 topological insulator is also a first decisive experiment following a compact theory, so the comparison between us is mainly about age and attribution, not about novelty.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B006 with Katori and Ye, argues that the lattice clock is a distinct invention with a clear lineage, would accept B004 as a good outcome, but needs the 2D versus 3D scope and the overlap with the 2016 prize settled first.
responses.response: Those are the two questions I can address directly. On scope, the citation as I now word it is limited to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall phase and the Z2 time-reversal-invariant class, and it does not claim the three-dimensional materials work, so Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan are not displaced, though I accept that a reader may feel the gap. On overlap, the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and Hall conductance in broken time-reversal systems. I also accept the substance of Kroll's argument for B006: reproduction at several national laboratories, a magic-wavelength condition that is a genuine invention and not a refinement, and a natural two-name credit. If the experts confirm the magic-wavelength priority, I would regard a Katori-Ye prize as fully defensible.

responses.point: Johansson now prefers B006 and keeps B004 as her main alternative, says she is less certain than I am that the three names are complete, and would support B004 if condensed-matter colleagues show that the credit boundary can be drawn cleanly, because she defers to them on that.
responses.response: I appreciate the deference and want to be honest about what I can offer. I cannot show that the credit boundary is clean; I can show that it is no worse than several prizes the committee has already awarded, and that the core theory (Kane-Mele) and the core measurement (Molenkamp) are unambiguous. The Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents and BHZ contributions interlock, and I think the committee should say so in its justification instead of claiming a settled boundary. If the outside reports find that BHZ were essential to the experiment's design, I would prefer to see B006 chosen than to credit a trio that I could not defend.

uncertainties: Whether an expert report would show that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang were essential to what Molenkamp measured, which would make a three-name B004 hard to defend.
Whether the Z2 class is judged distinct enough from the 2016 topological prize; I think it is, but colleagues outside condensed matter see overlap.
Whether the magic-wavelength priority of Katori over Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups holds under an expert report, which I cannot judge from memory.
Whether the resolution of the pairing mechanism or a second clean moire platform would change my view of B009 in the next few years.
How much weight a prize committee should give a new state of matter over a precision-measurement invention when both are well reproduced; this is a judgment I cannot reduce to evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I report no personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori or Ye. My field of first-principles magnetism and electronic structure is adjacent to topological and moire materials, which may bias me toward B004 and B009, and I disclose that. The overlaps disclosed by Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Olsson do not affect my participation on B004, B006 or B009.
